query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Thermal aging (>300°C for an extended period) of the non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA promotes diffusion-driven phase separation that precipitates Ti-rich intermetallic phases (e.g., Ti2Zn) at microstructural heterogeneities. These precipitates then serve as nucleation sites for a modified oxide scale (comprising enhanced TiO2 and MgO formation) that improves high-temperature oxidation resistance, while their heterogeneous distribution increases micro-galvanic coupling and leads to more localized corrosion in chloride-containing environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium microstructure produced via high-energy ball milling (HEBM) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) that contains a refined solid solution with metastable phase distributions and minimal intermetallic precipitation.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled thermal aging at temperatures above 300°C for a prolonged period.
generation.conditions: Aging followed by exposure to chloride-containing corrosive media and high-temperature oxidation tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation and growth of Ti-rich intermetallic phases, notably Ti2Zn, along with the formation of composite oxide scales (TiO2 and MgO) localized near micropores and phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Thermal aging increases atomic diffusion and drives phase separation, causing Ti to segregate and form intermetallic compounds. These intermetallics both promote a more protective, composite oxide film during oxidation (via enhanced TiO2 formation) and create localized cathodic sites, thereby intensifying micro-galvanic corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-processed (metastable) baseline, the aged alloy will exhibit a modified oxide layer with higher TiO2 content, improved high-temperature oxidation resistance, and increased local corrosion rates due to enhanced micro-galvanic effects.
generation.baseline: As-processed non-equilibrium alloy with a homogeneous metastable phase distribution and minimal Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates.
generation.boundary: The predicted effects are expected only when aging is performed above 300°C for sufficient durations to permit phase precipitation; variations in composition or processing history may alter the extent of these transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The precise volume fraction and spatial distribution of the Ti-rich intermetallics and how they quantitatively affect corrosion kinetics remain uncertain, as minor compositional or processing variations may influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples using HEBM and SPS. Subject one set to thermal aging at >300°C for a defined prolonged period, while maintaining the other set as the non-aged control. Subsequently, expose both sets to identical chloride-containing corrosive environments and high-temperature oxidation conditions. Use microscopy (SEM/TEM), XRD, and XPS to analyze phase evolutions and oxide scale compositions, and perform electrochemical testing (PDP, EIS) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to measure corrosion and oxidation behaviors.
measurements: Quantification of Ti-rich intermetallic phase fraction via XRD and TEM
Surface chemical analysis and oxide scale composition using XPS
Electrochemical measurements (PDP curves and impedance) to assess corrosion behavior
Oxidation rate constants from TGA under high-temperature cycling conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal aging treatment does not result in a statistically significant increase in Ti-rich intermetallic formation or the expected modification of the oxide scale, and if neither an improvement in high-temperature oxidation resistance nor an increase in localized corrosion is observed compared to the as-processed baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Among these systems, titanium (Ti) and zinc (Zn) have been reported to enhance the corrosion resistance of Mg alloys [,] by promoting the formation of intermetallic phases that act as corrosion barriers [,]. In combination with Zn, Ti can form stable intermetallic compounds, such as Ti2Zn and TiZn16, which provide a shielding effect and limit the progression of corrosion fronts [,]. In contrast, micro-galvanic effects between intermetallics and the Mg matrix, arising from electrochemical potential differences, can accelerate localized corrosion [,]. For example, Ti rich intermetallics may act as cathodic sites, enhancing the localized anodic dissolution of Mg [,]. This makes the spatial distribution, morphology, and size of these phases critical for determining corrosion performance []. Consequently, Mg-Ti-Zn alloys are promising for applications requiring both biocompatibility and corrosion resistance, especially in medical devices, where controlled degradation minimizes toxic byproduct formation [,]. cited_evidence.text: The microstructures of both alloys produced by SPS, along with the ball-milled powders, are shown in Figure 1. Low-magnification SEM images (Figure 1a,e) revealed numerous micropores in both alloys. High-magnification images (Figure 1c,g) show that the regions near the micropores were different in the two alloys. EDXS analysis revealed Mg-lean and Ti-enriched regions near micropores in the TZ alloy (Figure 1d). Trace amounts of Fe were also detected in the TZ alloy but not in the 4TZ alloy. This contamination likely originated from the stainless-steel balls and milling jar. Such Fe contamination is commonly reported in long-duration milling and may contribute to localized corrosion in Mg-based systems due to the cathodic nature of Fe relative to Mg [,]. However, the Fe concentration observed in the TEM was below 3 at.% and limited to isolated regions. Ti rich phases were absent in the 4TZ alloy; however, regions with higher Mg content and lower Zn content were observed. The observed microstructural differences between the alloys highlight the combined influence of HEBM, SPS, and composition. The PDP curves revealed that both the 4TZ and TZ alloys were more corrosion resistant than pure Mg. Both PDP and optical microscopy during immersion tests indicated that TZ was more corrosion resistant than the 4TZ alloy. The presence of Ti2Zn in the TZ alloys could be attributed to the increased corrosion resistance. Şuctic et al. demonstrated that Ti rich intermetallics in Zn alloys act as corrosion barriers, stabilizing the surrounding matrix []. Similarly, Ti2Zn may have helped stabilize the Mg matrix by acting as a barrier, probably forming inert islands of TiOx, slowing the propagation of corrosion fronts, while also promoting localized anodic dissolution of Mg due to galvanic interactions. This localized effect, along with the distribution of Ti rich phases around micropores, may have created cathodic sites, leading to variations in corrosion susceptibility across the alloy.

Initially, a mixed surface film of MgO, ZnO, and TiO2 was formed during immersion. This film passivates portions of the surface, but breakdown occurs at weak points, especially near pores or compositional heterogeneities. Localized Mg dissolution initiates where the film fails, and Fe-rich inclusions may accelerate this process by acting as cathodic sites. Ti2Zn intermetallics act as partial barriers to corrosion front propagation, although they may also participate in galvanic coupling. In contrast, the more uniform phase distribution in 4TZ leads to slower localized degradation. This model represents one possible interpretation of corrosion behavior based on the current data. Future work using advanced surface-sensitive techniques, such as angle-resolved XPS, SIMS, or high-resolution cross-sectional TEM, could reveal the detailed structure and layering of these oxide films and validate the assumptions underlying this proposed mechanism.
